question: What is the scientific name of Ginger?
expected_check: Name should be Zingiber officinale; answer briefly.
answer: The scientific name of Ginger is Zingiber officinale.

Document 1: Name (English): Ginger
Name (Sinhala): ඉඟුරු / Ginger
Scientific Name: Zingiber officinale
Family Name: Zingiberaceae
Medicinal Usage: Ginger root, and especially the leaves, are used to treat anorexia, indigestion, loss of appetite, flatulence, hyperacidity, cough, asthma, hiccups, dysentery, gout, sciatica, and blood in urine.
When used medicinally, ginger root is dried according to accepted methods and the dried ginger is called Siddhi Ginger or Siddha Ginger. Ginger has properties that relieve cold, relieve pain, reduce swelling, stimulate the nerves, calm the wind, improve memory, stimulate appetite, and increase hunger.
Plant Part Used: Ginger root, leaves,
Preparation: For loss of appetite and lack of appetite, a little raw ginger should be taken with salt or sea salt before eating. For colds, mouth ulcers and constipation, ginger, black pepper, and tippili powder should be taken with ginger juice and gargled and the mouth should be rinsed to remove phlegm. For headaches, raw ginger is grated and applied to the nose. For dysentery, raw ginger and iriveriya are boiled and given to drink. For chronic asthma and flatulence, a decoction of dried ginger is used. For urination, a decoction of dried ginger is given. For phlegm, irritation, and constipation, drinking ginger juice mixed with honey is beneficial.
Precautions/Limitations: High doses may cause heartburn or interact with blood-thinning medication; caution is advised for individuals with gallstones or bleeding disorders; consult a doctor before regular medicinal use during pregnancy.
Scientific Evidence Level: Supported by clinical studies for nausea (pregnancy, post-operative); chemotherapy-induced nausea results are mixed; other traditional uses are not clinically verified.
Evidence by Use: Nausea in pregnancy: meta-analyses show reduced nausea, with no significant effect on vomiting frequency. Post-operative nausea and vomiting: meta-analyses show lower incidence than placebo. Chemotherapy-induced nausea: mixed trial results. Indigestion, cough, asthma, gout and other listed uses: traditional use.
Evidence References: [1] Viljoen E, Visser J, Koen N, Musekiwa A. A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect and safety of ginger in the treatment of pregnancy-associated nausea and vomiting. Nutr J. 2014;13:20. PMID 24642205. | [2] Efficacy of ginger in preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Nurs Scholarsh. 2021;53(6):671-679. doi:10.1111/jnu.12691. | [3] Marx W, Teleni L, McCarthy AL, Vitetta L, McKavanagh D, Thomson D, Isenring E. Ginger (Zingiber officinale) and chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting: a systematic literature review. Nutr Rev. 2013;71(4):245-254. | [4] Paudel KR, Orent J, Penela OG. Pharmacological properties of ginger (Zingiber officinale): what do meta-analyses say? A systematic review. Front Pharmacol. 2025;16:1619655. doi:10.3389/fphar.2025.1619655.

Document 2: Name (English): Turmeric
Name (Sinhala): කහ / Turmeric
Scientific Name: Curcuma longa
Family Name: Zingiberaceae
Medicinal Usage: Turmeric is commonly used to treat skin diseases, fungal infections, pimples and other skin enhancement therapies. 
Plant Part Used: The rhizome (underground stem or root) 
Preparation: For skin diseases, turmeric and neem (Azadirachta indica) leaves are boiled together and water extract is used to wash the infected areas. For the fungal infections of the skin, ground raw turmeric and Aththora (Cassia alanta) past is applied. A mixture of ground turmeric along with undupiyaliya (Desmondium triflorum) is applied for pimples. Also, turmeric’s anti-inflammatory, antiseptic and expectorant properties give the ability to fight against cold and chest ailments speedily 
Precautions/Limitations: May cause skin irritation in sensitive individuals; not a substitute for medical treatment of deep, infected, or non-healing wounds; high internal doses may interact with blood-thinning medication, so caution is advised for people on anticoagulants.
Scientific Evidence Level: Traditional use with preliminary-to-moderate clinical evidence for some skin conditions (psoriasis, itching, scarring); other traditional uses not clinically verified.
Evidence by Use: Skin conditions (psoriasis, pruritus, scarring): randomized trials of turmeric/curcumin products show benefit, but trials are small and use standardized products, not the traditional boiled turmeric-neem wash. Fungal skin infection and acne: very limited trial evidence. Cold and chest ailments: traditional use only.
Evidence References: [1] Vaughn AR, Branum A, Sivamani RK. Effects of turmeric (Curcuma longa) on skin health: a systematic review of the clinical evidence. Phytother Res. 2016;30(8):1243-1264. PMID 27213821. | [2] Patel P, Wang JY, Mineroff J, Jagdeo J. Evaluation of curcumin for dermatologic conditions: a systematic review. Arch Dermatol Res. 2023;316(1):37. PMID 38085369.

Document 3: Name (English): Asamodagam
Name (Sinhala): අසමෝදගම් / Asamodagam
Scientific Name: Trachyspermum roxburghianum
Family Name: Apiaceae
Medicinal Usage: Asamodagam soothes inflamed phlegm and wind. Relieves pain. Strengthens the nerves. Stimulates the heart. Good for coughs. Diuretic. Increases appetite. 
Plant Part Used: Asamodagam leaves, plant
Preparation: Asamodagam spirit is an effective remedy for flatulence and indigestion in young children. Roasting Asamodagam seeds in boiling water, leaving them for a while and giving a little of the water to drink cures indigestion and diarrhea in young children. Asamodagam is used with other medicines for eye diseases, vomiting, hiccups and urinary diseases, insect diseases, intestinal diseases, dysentery, gout, increased acidity of the stomach and indigestion. As a home remedy, boiling anise and ginger together and giving them to drink for indigestion, applying a paste made from grinding anise seeds for swelling, applying Asamodagam oil for pain, grinding the seeds and inhaling the smoke for asthma, and eating Asamodagam leaves raw as a sambal are very beneficial.
Precautions/Limitations: Should be given to children only in very small amounts; excessive intake may cause digestive irritation; not a substitute for medical treatment of chronic respiratory or digestive conditions.
Scientific Evidence Level: Traditional/folk use; limited formal research.

Document 4: Name (English): Nutmeg
Name (Sinhala): සාදික්කා / Sadikka
Scientific Name: Myristica fragrans Houtt
Family Name: Myristicaceae
Medicinal Usage: It is especially used for making various flavoring products. It is also used in the production of perfumes, soaps, ointments and similar products, where the resin and essential oil extracted from Sadikka are utilized. Sadikka can also be used to produce food and beverage products.
Sadikka is used medicinally to treat conditions such as gas accumulation in the abdomen, nausea, vomiting, cleansing, indigestion, oral diseases, sinusitis, hiccups, fever and other ailments. People in various countries also use Sadikka for treating paralysis, nervous diseases, insomnia, drug overdose, pain relief and more
Plant Part Used:
Preparation: When indigestion causes bloating, drinking Sadikka powder in a small amount of citrus juice or warm water is an effective remedy. It is also beneficial for vomiting, deafness and wind diseases. Sadikka shows antibacterial and anti-paralysis properties. It is helpful in controlling high blood pressure. Sadikka contains highly toxic poison. Therefore, death can occur if taken in excessive amounts.
Precautions/Limitations: Nutmeg contains myristicin, which is toxic in large amounts and can cause hallucinations, rapid heartbeat, nausea, or severe poisoning; only small culinary/medicinal amounts should ever be used; not recommended for children, pregnant women, or as a self-medicated treatment for nervous or psychiatric conditions.
Scientific Evidence Level: Traditional use; toxicity at high doses is well documented in medical literature.

Document 5: Name (English): Venivel / Calumba
Name (Sinhala): වෙනිවැල් / 
Scientific Name: Coscinium fenestratum
Family Name: Menispermaceae
Medicinal Usage: Venivel is a very bitter herb used for diabetes, fever, jaundice, and skin diseases. It has strong anti-diabetic, anti-inflammatory, and anti-malarial properties. It is also used to treat peptic ulcers, dysentery, and as a general bitter tonic for appetite.
Plant Part Used: Stem (wood)
Preparation: A small piece of the stem is boiled in water until the water turns yellow. This decoction is taken in small doses (2–3 teaspoons) twice daily for diabetes and fever. Externally, the paste is applied to wounds and skin infections.
Precautions/Limitations: May cause digestive discomfort in high doses due to its bitterness; people on diabetes medication should monitor blood sugar due to its blood-sugar-lowering effect; not a substitute for confirmed antimalarial treatment.
Scientific Evidence Level: Traditional use; antidiabetic, antimicrobial and wound-healing activity shown in animal and laboratory studies only; the plant is endangered, so use is restricted.
Evidence by Use: Diabetes, bacterial infections, wound healing: reported in animal and in vitro studies; human trials of the whole plant were not found. Its constituent berberine has separate human data, which should not be attributed to the plant itself. Fever, jaundice, skin diseases, peptic ulcers, dysentery: traditional use.
Evidence References: [1] Danapur V, Haleshi C, Sringeswara AN. Endangered medicinal plant Coscinium fenestratum (Gaertn.) Colebr. - a review. Pharmacogn J. 2020;12(5):1077-1085. doi:10.5530/pj.2020.12.152. | [2] Shirwaikar A, Rajendran K, Punitha ISR. Antidiabetic activity of alcoholic stem extract of Coscinium fenestratum in streptozotocin-nicotinamide induced type 2 diabetic rats. J Ethnopharmacol. 2005;97(2):369-374. | [3] Goveas SW, Abraham A. Evaluation of antimicrobial and antioxidant activity of stem and leaf extracts of Coscinium fenestratum.

question: ගොටුකොල සාම්ප්‍රදායිකව භාවිතා කරන්නේ කුමක් සඳහාද?
expected_check: Traditional uses; avoid unsupported clinical claims.
answer:
ගොටුකොල සාම්ප්‍රදායිකව මතකය වැඩිදියුණු කිරීම, සමේ රෝග හා තුවාල සම්බන්ධ භාවිතයන් සඳහා ප්‍රසිද්ධය. අධි රුධිර පීඩනය, රුධිර සංසරණය, ස්නායු ආශ්‍රිත තත්ත්වයන්, ආතතිය හා කනස්සල්ල සඳහාද භාවිතා කරයි. 

ඉතා දිගුකාලීන අධික මාත්‍රාවලදී හිසරදය, බඩේ අපහසුතා හෝ හිරු එළියට සමේ සංවේදීතාව වැඩි විය හැක. ගර්භණී අවධියේ වෛද්‍ය උපදෙස් නොමැතිව විශාල ප්‍රමාණවලින් භාවිත නොකළ යුතුය.

question: What does clinical research say about Gotukola and memory?
expected_check: Cognitive benefit is not confirmed by the recorded trials.
answer:
Gotukola, scientifically known as Centella asiatica and belonging to the Apiaceae family, is traditionally reported to improve memory. However, clinical research indicates that a meta-analysis of randomized trials found no significant difference from placebo regarding cognitive outcomes. Therefore, the support for memory enhancement is primarily traditional, with no confirmed clinical evidence.

There are also preliminary clinical studies indicating its effectiveness in wound healing, but more trials are needed to establish this firmly. The evidence for anxiety and stress relief is mainly derived from animal studies.

Toxicity concerns include potential headaches, stomach upset, or increased skin sensitivity to sunlight with prolonged high-dose use, and large amounts should be avoided during pregnancy without medical advice.

Evidence References:
[1] Arribas-Lopez E, Zand Fard N, Ojo O, Snowden M, Kochhar T. A systematic review of the effect of Centella asiatica on wound healing. question: What is the evidence for Ginger helping nausea?
expected_check: Evidence qualification and limitations must be grounded.
answer:
Ginger (Zingiber officinale) has evidence supporting its effectiveness in helping with nausea, particularly in specific contexts:

- Nausea in pregnancy: Meta-analyses indicate that ginger reduces nausea, although it does not significantly affect the frequency of vomiting.
- Post-operative nausea and vomiting: Meta-analyses show that ginger leads to a lower incidence of nausea compared to placebo.
- Chemotherapy-induced nausea: The results from trials are mixed, indicating varying effectiveness.

References for these findings include systematic reviews and meta-analyses published in reputable journals.

question: What are the precautions and contraindications for Neem oil?
expected_check: Toxicity particularly for children; avoid invented dosage.
answer:
Plant part and preparation: Neem oil is obtained from the seeds of the Azadirachta indica tree. It is yellow in color, bitter, acrid, and has an unpleasant odor. 

Indications: Traditionally used for various conditions including skin diseases, ulcers, leprosy, and blood disorders.

Precautions and contraindications: Neem oil and seed extracts can be toxic if ingested in large amounts, particularly in infants and young children. It is not recommended during pregnancy and may cause allergic skin reactions in some individuals. Neem oil is intended for external/topical use rather than internal consumption.

Evidence strength: Traditional use with laboratory-level evidence for antibacterial and antifungal activity; clinical efficacy for skin disease not established; toxicity risk at high doses.

question: More Information About Murraya Koenigii Insect Damage
expected_check: Should explain verified curry leaf pest symptoms.
answer:
About the condition: Murraya koenigii, commonly known as curry leaf, can suffer from insect damage. This refers to a range of injuries caused by various insects rather than a specific disease.

Symptoms to look for: You may notice small pinholes or nibbling on tender leaves, irregular or geometric chewing cuts, partial defoliation, yellowing or curling of leaves due to sap feeding, and sometimes a black sooty coating from honeydew.

Healthy leaf comparison: Healthy curry leaf leaflets should be intact and green, without any feeding holes, major cut-outs, yellowing, curling, or sooty deposits.

Recommended actions: Avoid using heavily insect-damaged leaves for any medicinal preparations. Regularly inspect tender shoots and both sides of the leaflets, remove any severely infested material, and identify the pest before deciding on a control method.

References: 
- https://www.researchgate.net/publication/379255673_Record_of_new_pests_of_curry_leaves_Murraya_koenigii_L_Spreng_from_Kerala_India 
- https://www.researchgate.net/publication/376314456_Phytochemical_Profiling_of_Primary_and_Secondary_Metabolites_in_Pest_Infested_Murraya_koenigii_L_Spreng

Recommended Action: Do not use heavily insect-damaged leaves for medicinal preparation. Inspect tender shoots and both sides of leaflets, remove severely infested material, and identify the pest before choosing a control method.

question: More Information About Centella Asiatica WormCreep
expected_check: Should explain caterpillar damage, not medicinal uses.
answer:
About the condition: The plant Centella asiatica is affected by a condition known as Worm Creep Damage. This is primarily caused by caterpillar feeding, leading to abnormal damage rather than being a disease caused by pathogens.

Symptoms to look for: You should look for signs such as chewed or missing leaf tissue, progressive feeding on both young and older leaves, ragged leaf edges, partial defoliation, and in severe cases, extensive loss of leaves, leaving mainly stems or petioles.

Healthy leaf comparison: Healthy Centella asiatica leaves appear intact, green, and spreading, without signs of extensive chewing, missing tissue, ragged margins, or progressive defoliation.

Recommended actions: Avoid using heavily caterpillar-damaged, contaminated, or partly decomposed leaves for any medicinal preparation. Instead, select intact healthy leaves after addressing the pest issue. Inspect both leaf surfaces and nearby growth for caterpillars and their eggs, and hand-pick small populations where possible. Remove any severely damaged leaves. If control measures are needed, use only products registered for the crop and pest, such as caterpillar-specific biological controls, and follow all label and pre-harvest instructions.

References: 
- https://doi.org/10.3390/agriengineering6010037 
- https://www.extension.umd.edu/resource/caterpillars-trees 
- https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9241546271 
- https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241500739

question: ගොටුකොල මතකය වැඩි කරන බවට ඇති විද්‍යාත්මක සාක්ෂි පර්යේෂකයෙකු ලෙස පැහැදිලි කරන්න.
expected_check: Verify language, researcher persona, evidence and references.
answer:
Scientific Name: Centella asiatica  
Family Name: Apiaceae  

Gotukola is traditionally reported to improve memory, but the scientific evidence is limited. A meta-analysis of randomized trials found no significant difference from placebo regarding cognitive outcomes, indicating that the cognitive benefits of Gotukola are not confirmed. 

Evidence for wound healing is based on preliminary clinical studies, with a systematic review identifying four clinical trials showing signs of improved healing, although more research is needed. Evidence for anxiety reduction is primarily derived from animal studies.

Toxicity concerns include potential headaches, stomach upset, or increased skin sensitivity to sunlight with prolonged high-dose use. It is advised to avoid large amounts during pregnancy without medical advice.

Evidence References:

[2] Puttarak P, Dilokthornsakul P, Saokaew S, et al. Effects of Centella asiatica (L.) Urb. on cognitive function and mood related outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sci Rep. 2017;7:10646. doi:10.1038/s41598-017-09823-9.  
[3] Sun B, Wu L, Wu Y, Zhang C, Qin L, Hayashi M, Kudo M, Gao M, Liu T. Therapeutic potential of Centella asiatica and its triterpenes: a review. Front Pharmacol. 2020;11:568032. doi:10.3389/fphar.2020.568032.
